extracted.intended_audience: economists and policy researchers studying the interaction between health shocks and socioeconomic status using panel survey data (e.g., HRS/AHEAD)
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical framework and measurement guidelines for estimating consequences of new health events (onsets of chronic conditions) for out-of-pocket medical expenses, labor supply, income, insurance, and wealth, and for testing whether SES predicts future health, using HRS panel data and multi-wave models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of major vs minor chronic conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Major conditions were defined as cancer, heart condition, stroke, and diseases of the lung. All other onsets are defined as minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major trumps minor: an individual reporting both a minor and major onset is included in the major category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'new health event' (health shock)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'new health event' is the onset of a new chronic condition between survey waves (an innovation in health Ht).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To consider the onset as an exogenous 'news' health shock, include predictors of onset in models so remaining statistical variation in new onsets is plausibly unanticipated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification requirement for causal inference (exogenous variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate causal effects of health on SES (and vice versa) one requires exogenous variation in health (or SES) that is not induced by SES (health).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use onset of new chronic conditions as the best available health shocks, but control for predictors of onset; for estimating SES→health, exploit exogenous wealth increases (e.g., unanticipated stock market wealth gains) as plausibly exogenous variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline controls (X) required in models
rubrics_metrics.description: Models should control for a vector of baseline attributes: birth cohort (age), marital status, race, ethnicity, education, region, family income quintiles, and baseline health measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline health measures include dummies for self-reported health status, presence of each chronic condition, behavioral risk factors (smoking, exercise, BMI, drinking), and a scaled index of functional limitations (ADL). Including these increases confidence that new onsets capture unexpected shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction to survivors
rubrics_metrics.description: All models in the paper are restricted to survivors—those who neither attrited nor died across the waves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ignores relationships of SES with attrition and mortality (mortality selection may be important particularly in older cohorts such as AHEAD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome variables to measure consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate impacts of new health events on out-of-pocket (OOP) medical expenses, possession/type of health insurance, labor supply (probability of working), hours worked conditional on working, household income, and household wealth/savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure OOP medical expenses both cumulatively across waves and period-by-period; household income is measured for previous year; wealth change can be measured directly or approximated by cumulative income loss plus OOP medical expenses (plus foregone interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal/dynamic modeling across waves
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate a series of equations for adjacent-wave changes in each outcome (e.g., ΔL_t = ... + Σ β_i ΔH_{t-i}) including lagged health shocks as covariates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows distinguishing contemporaneous single-period effects from multi-period spillovers: if only contemporaneous effects exist, lagged coefficients will be zero. Empirically, major health events show a large immediate effect followed by diminishing additional effects in later waves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity classification and heterogeneous effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish health events by severity (severe vs minor) because different kinds of health changes have different economic consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severe events (major) produce much larger mean and right-tail OOP increases and larger reductions in labor force participation than minor events; analyses should stratify by severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of health insurance status
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for baseline health insurance status and changes in insurance (types) when estimating medical cost consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Health insurance dampens but does not eliminate OOP costs; stratify OOP distributions by baseline insurance. New major events often trigger shifts from employer coverage toward government coverage (Medicare) — include insurance type transitions in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement strategy for wealth effects (cumulative model vs direct wealth change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two alternative measures of savings/wealth change: (1) cumulative income loss plus cumulative OOP medical expenses (plus foregone interest) and (2) direct change in household wealth between waves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cumulative income+OOP measure is less contaminated by measurement error and capital gains and typically yields higher R² and more precise estimates; direct wealth change is noisier with larger standard errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stock-market-induced wealth changes as exogenous SES variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use large, presumably unanticipated increases in stock market wealth during the 1990s as a source of exogenous variation in household wealth to test whether financial SES improvements affect subsequent health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instrument/strategy is limited because such increases are concentrated among the wealthy; other credible exogenous SES changes spanning the distribution would be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing interactions and heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Test interaction effects of a new health onset with race, gender, ethnicity, education, income, and wealth to detect heterogeneous impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study interactions were generally insignificant except that higher baseline wealth (or income) amplified the reduction in wealth growth following a major health onset, consistent with consumption smoothing/liquidity constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probit specification for predicting new onset (predictors of future disease)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict future onset of major/minor chronic conditions using probit models that control for baseline self-reported health (excellent/very good/good/fair/poor), presence of baseline chronic conditions, functional limitations scale, behavioral risk factors (smoking, vigorous exercise, BMI quadratic), demographic controls (cohort, race, Hispanic, sex, region), and SES measures (household income, household wealth, education dummies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education (12–15 years, 16+ years) is strongly predictive of future onset even after controlling baseline health; household income never predicts onset over the ~8-year horizon; wealth has at best weak/condition-specific predictive power. Include units and missing-value indicators; report chi-squares and statistical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation cautions and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about limitations: measurement error in wealth, potential mortality selection, timing assumptions (e.g., health event assumed to occur midway between waves for income loss calculation), and concentration of exogenous wealth changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats affect interpretation: cumulative income losses often exceed cumulative OOP costs; measurement error biases coefficients when income/wealth appear on both sides of equations; AHEAD (older sample with Medicare) shows smaller wealth impacts from health events so results may not generalize across ages.
